metadata.title: The Shader Math Toolkit
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: A dozen small functions behind shader effects
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation (built-in functions); Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro, Forward+ (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: The Shader Math Toolkit. Learn a dozen small functions that shape what a shader draws, then use three of them to build a soft ring.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. People think shaders need advanced math. They need about a dozen small functions, and each one reshapes a smooth run of numbers. Learn what each does, and you can predict what a shader will draw.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A pixel is one dot of the picture. U V is a point's address on a shape: zero to one across, zero to one down. A function takes numbers in and gives one number out. And a vector is a bundle of two to four numbers.

beats.narration_text: This ring is not an image. Three small functions draw it: one measures distance, one softens an edge, one blends two colors. By the end, you will be able to read every line of it.

beats.narration_text: Start with a ramp: a smooth run of values from zero up to one. The simplest ramp is a pixel's address across the shape: zero at the left edge, one at the right. In code, that is U V dot x.

Under the strip, in mono: 'UV.x · across the shape'. Caption in serif, the GLOSSARY wording: 'ramp · a smooth run of values from 0 up to 1'.

Mono formula tag 'f(x) = x'. A small gray credit under the plot: 'curves drawn from the formulas · checked against Godot 4.7.2 renders'.

beats.narration_text: About a dozen functions come in three families. Cut and blend: step, smooth step, mix, clamp. Repeat and fold: abs, fract, floor, mod. Distance and curves: length, normalize, distance, power, sine. Then we use three of them to build a ring.

At the right a ring outline; thin lines run from the chips distance, smoothstep and mix to it.

beats.narration_text: Step is a switch. Give it an edge and a ramp. Where the ramp is below the edge, the answer is zero. At the edge or above, it is one. The plot is a single jump.

Mono tag 'step(edge, x) · 0 below the edge, 1 from the edge up' (the GLOSSARY wording). Strip beneath: left half black tiles, right half white tiles.

beats.narration_text: In a shader, the edge goes first, then the ramp. Here the edge is a uniform, a dial your game can turn from outside. Slide it, and the hard split slides with it.

The split slides left and right as the edge dial is swept.

beats.narration_text: Clamp pins a number inside a range. Below the low end, you get the low end. Above the high end, you get the high end. In between, nothing changes. It is max first, then min.

shot.visual_intent: The standard plot with two horizontal guide lines at y = 0 and y = 1 labelled 'low end' and 'high end'. A dashed overshooting ramp y = 2x - 0.5 runs from (0, -0.5) to (1, 1.5) beyond the guides; the solid curve is clamp(2x - 0.5, 0, 1): flat at 0 until x = 0.25, a ramp to 1 at x = 0.75, flat at 1 after. Short labels 'max · the higher of two' and 'min · the lower of two' on the two ends, mono tag 'clamp(x, low, high) = min(max(x, low), high)'. Strip beneath: black tiles, a ramp of tiles, white tiles.

beats.narration_text: The docs spell out the formula. Squeeze the input between the edges into zero to one, call that t, and return three t squared minus two t cubed. They also warn that a first edge at or above the second gives undefined results.

Ring and camera numbers are fitted to the real capture.

beats.narration_text: Mix slides between two values. Give it a start, an end, and a weight. Weight zero returns the start, one returns the end, one half lands halfway. It does not pin the weight: a weight of two overshoots the end, so clamp it first.

shot.visual_intent: The standard plot with the weight (the ramp, axis label 't · weight') as input from 0 to 2 and the output going from a start value to an end value: a straight line from (0, 0.2) through (1, 0.9), continuing dashed to (2, 1.6); tick labels 'a · start' and 'b · end' on the y axis at 0.2 and 0.9. Read-outs on the line at weights 0, 1 and one half: 'start', 'end', 'halfway'; then at weight 2 the read-out 'overshoots: 1.6'. Mono tag 'mix(a, b, t) · blends from a to b: t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b' (the GLOSSARY wording) and a smaller 'a x (1 - t) + b x t'. A small bracket 'clamp(t, 0, 1)' lands on the weight axis between 0 and 1. Strip beneath, for weights 0 to 1 only, from the gray of 0.2 up to the gray of 0.9.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A ramp is a smooth run from zero to one, and every function reshapes it. Step cuts, smooth step cuts softly, mix blends, clamp pins. Abs folds, fract repeats, floor counts, mod repeats at any length. Length and distance measure, normalize keeps a direction, power bends a curve. Distance, smooth step and mix together draw a ring. Read the line of a function and you can predict the picture.

Is the ring round and centered? And does the radius dial move the ring in and out, with soft edges?
